Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for joining this meeting to commemorate and promote the International Day Against Nuclear Tests. As we mark the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, we must also acknowledge a sobering parallel. 80 years since the first ever nuclear test explosion in New Mexico and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the UN's legacy remains indelibly linked to one of the darkest chapters in human history. It is a legacy we cannot disavow. But it is also a solemn reminder or one of our core missions to prevent the scourge of war and the threat of nuclear annihilation. While progress has been made, nuclear disarmament is not a task that ends. Your Excellencies, our efforts must remain continuous and resolute. If we want to rid the world of nuclear weapons, we must first halt nuclear testing. Nuclear testing not only has the potential to lead to a dangerous nuclear arms race, its consequences also have devastating impacts on people and planet. The International Day Against Nuclear Testing reflects these realities. Recognized each year on 29 August, the International Day commemorates the closing of the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site in Kazakhstan nearly a quarter century ago. The closing of the site was one of many moments that put an end to a decades-long rush to build and expand nuclear arsenals. It reflected a deeper understanding and willingness to limit and work to halt nuclear testing. On this International Day, I call upon all Member States that have not yet signed and ratified the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to do so without delay. In particular, I urge the remaining states that participated in the 1996 negotiations of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty at the Conference on Disarmament and that possessed nuclear power to research reactors at that time to move forward with ratification. This step is not only overdue, for the entry into force of this important treaty, it is essential for our collective security. Your Excellencies, between 1945 and 1996, more than 2,000 nuclear tests were conducted worldwide, leaving behind grave health consequences and enduring environmental contamination. This cannot be allowed to continue. The risks are far too great. The opening for signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty in 1996 proved effective. It led to a significant reduction in nuclear testing. Indeed, since 1996, fewer than a dozen nuclear tests have taken place. The Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty is thus a great example of how diplomacy, together with science, can enhance global security. Here I commend the tireless efforts of the Preparatory Commission for the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization, CTBTO. I also wish to commend the contributions of Member States to its international monitoring system, which continues to safeguard the world by detecting potential nuclear tests. Your Excellencies, we must overcome the syndrome under which we are always willing to pay for war, but not for peace. Let today be an opportunity to reject the drift toward rearmament and instead firmly commit to dialogue, diplomacy, and collective action. We made a promise last year in the Pact for the Future to achieve the total elimination of nuclear weapons. Let us continue on the path that we started in 1996 and renew our determination to prohibit nuclear testing as a first and important step towards nuclear disarmament. And let us do it by making sure that 30 years after its opening for signature, the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty finally enters into force. Thank you. In accordance with Rule 70 of the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly, I now give the floor to Ms. Izumi Nakamitsu, Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs, who will deliver a statement on behalf of the Secretary-General, His Excellency Antonio Guterres.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, at the outset, allow me to extend my sincere gratitude to the President of the General Assembly, His Excellency Mr. Philemon Young, for convening this important annual commemoration. I also want to thank Kazakhstan, for its leadership and unwavering commitment to ensuring that the devastating legacy of nuclear tests is never forgotten. By initiating this day, Kazakhstan provided the world with not only a moment for remembrance, but also a platform for action. And I take this opportunity to commend the Preparatory Commission for the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization and its Provisional Technical Secretariat. Their tireless efforts to sustain the norm against nuclear testing through advancing the Treaty's universalization and in strengthening the verification regime are indispensable to our collective security. Excellencies, Today's commemoration takes place in a world overshadowed by conflict, mistrust, and the looming shadow of nuclear weapons. Trust between states continues to erode, while investments in nuclear weapons and their delivery systems increase. Against this backdrop, the prohibition of all nuclear explosive testing is not merely a technical or procedural matter. It is a moral and strategic necessity. The CTBT is one of the most widely supported instruments in the disarmament and non-proliferation regime. The expansion and proven reliability of the International Monitoring System, IMS, and the International Data Center, IDC, are remarkable achievements. Together, they have helped reassure the world of the absence of nuclear tests and detected those who have sought to violate this global norm. Yet, nearly three decades after its adoption, the CTBT has not yet entered into force, and the totality of its promise remains unrealized. This relay cannot continue. Let me be clear, the only path to abolishing nuclear tests is through a legally binding prohibition, respected, implemented, and above all, enforced. That is the promise of the CTBT. It is incumbent upon every state to bring that promise to life, but in particular those states whose ratification is still required for the treaty's entry into force. Their leadership will decide whether this treaty finally closes the door on the era of nuclear testing. In the meantime, the global moratorium on nuclear testing must hold. It embodies our shared commitment to the norm against nuclear tests. Nuclear testing can never be permitted, not as a tool of deterrence, not as a display of political influence, not under the guise of science. The consequences of nuclear tests are indiscriminate and enduring. They have left behind wounds, human, environmental, and moral, that can never be fully healed. Survivors of nuclear testing remind us of the truth every day. Their suffering is not confined to history books. It continues in the present. Families and communities endure intergenerational harm, underscoring the cruelty of these weapons. Their voices obligate us to ensure that no community bears such burden ever again. The recent establishment of an independent scientific panel to study the effects of nuclear war is a clear acknowledgement by the international community of the enduring humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons. It reflects a growing recognition that human, environmental and health impacts of nuclear explosions, whether in war or in testing, must be properly scrutinized through the lens of dispassionate science. Distinguished delegates, as the Secretary-General has said, the world must speak with one voice to end nuclear testing once and for all. Nuclear tests have haunted our past. They scar our present. They must not define our future. From the steps of Semipalatinsk to the atolls of the Pacific, the earth still carries the burden of nuclear testing. But the measure of our commitment will not be found in the words we speak today. It will be found in the choices we make tomorrow. That choice is ours, and it must be to end nuclear testing forever. I thank you very much for your attention.

I thank the Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs. Before proceeding further, and as indicated in my letter dated 26 August 2025, I should like to consult Members with a view to inviting the following speakers to deliver keynote addresses at this commemorative meeting. Mr. Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization. Ms. Vivian Okeke, Director of the International Atomic Energy Agency Liaison Office in New York, on behalf of Mr. Rafael Mariano Grossi, Director General of the Agency. Ms. Uemva Johnson, Youth Representative from Kiribati. May I take it that it is the wish of the Assembly, without setting a precedent, to invite these speakers to make statements at this commemorative meeting? It is so decided. I give the floor to Mr. Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Mr. President, thank you for convening this session and for inviting me to address this General Assembly on this important day. My thanks also to Izumi Nakamitsu. Izumi is the Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs, and she's presented a wonderful opening remarks on behalf of the Secretary-General. Thank you. We've all just marked the somber 80th anniversary of the first nuclear test and the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings. I joined the commemoration events in Japan just last month. Standing on a mountain on the 8th of August, the eve of the commemoration, I looked down on the city of Nagasaki. That spot was about 500 meters from the original target location for the nuclear bomb. But it was a cloudy morning, and the pilot needed to have visual targeting on the ground. He could see three and a half kilometres further up the valley, and so he dropped the bomb there. Destruction reached out even to the original site. Seeing the city's lights twinkle, 80 years on, and thinking about the 70,000 people that had lost their lives by the end of that year made a strong impression on me. Eighty years is a long time. Eighty years from today goes into the next century to the 3rd of September of 2105. Since those first nuclear weapons were launched over Japan, in a full 80 years, the world has not seen even one nuclear weapon explode as an act of war. How to get through another 80 years to 2105 in the same way? Since 1945, after World War II ended, there were no more nuclear weapons exploding in war. That is true. But nuclear test explosions continued. Over the next 50 years, some 2,000 nuclear explosions. During the latter Cold War period, these massive nuclear test explosions averaged about one test every week. This had to stop. And it largely has stopped. Following the CTBT's opening for signature in 1996, fewer than a dozen tests have taken place. At the end of this month, we start celebrating the 30th anniversary year of this remarkable treaty and its opening for signature. It's been a triumph for science, for multilateralism, for our global environment, for humanity. Under the treaty, We've set up the international monitoring system, over 300 facilities around the planet, including stations and analytical laboratories. Just last month, a new station was certified in our network in the People's Republic of China. We're close to completing this powerful network. The system uses four different technology types. It listens to vibrations in the earth, in the sea, in the air and it sniffs the air for telltale radionuclides. Together, they will detect any suspected nuclear test and pinpoint its location to within a few kilometres. One key feature of this system, it can tell us with unchallengeable scientific precision that a nuclear explosion has taken place. It can also tell us with the same unchallengeable scientific precision that an event was not a nuclear explosion. This is all important for global security. We saw this just last year. Rumors and misinformation flew around the world following some earthquakes in northern Iran in October last year. Tensions and risks rose. The CTBTO soon showed beyond doubt that the events had been natural earthquakes and not a nuclear test. The misinformation, it stopped. And the tensions and the risks eased. This episode shows the immediate practical importance of the CTBT. Multilateralism delivering global benefits. The CTBTO delivering benefits. Under our national data centers for all initiative, more countries access the treaty's rich data streams and products. And this is to help detect nuclear tests for sure, but also for their own civil and scientific purposes. We invest in multilingualism, delivering training and other events around the world in different languages. We have a lively worldwide youth group, a mentoring program for young women in science, technology, engineering and maths disciplines from around the world. All this allows all states, bigger or smaller, to access the full benefits of treaty membership. Everyone can lend their voice to supporting a full and final ban on nuclear testing. But And as you all know, there is a significant but here. The CTBTO now has 187 signatories, 178 ratifications, a mighty international convergence of view. However, the treaty is still to enter into force. Under the treaty's annex two, 44 named states have to ratify the treaty. Nine are still yet to do so. We all know the international mood is much darker now. The solidarity and responsibility that saw the Treaty agreed in 1996 have given way to divisions, tensions, even threats. So as we enter the Treaty's 30th anniversary year, it's all the more important that all states stand firm on ending nuclear testing. Can we take two major policy steps. First, all nuclear-armed states maintain and reaffirm their respective moratoria on testing. And second, those states that have yet to sign and/or ratify the treaty think hard about the advantage of taking that all-important step towards universalising this treaty. the global goodwill and prestige, especially for those states that can bring us closer to entry into force. In July this year, 129 Nobel laureates, leading scientists and thinkers of the world, signed a declaration calling for these same two bold steps. At last year's commemoration of the International Day Against Nuclear Tests, I pointed out that if we get to the mid of January next year, 2026, without a nuclear test, we'll set a new record, the longest period without any test since the first Trinity test in New Mexico in 1945. A year has passed, we're closing in on that record. It's only a few months away now. Soon we'll be talking about a few weeks rather than months. But delegates, having set that record, let's extend it. If all goes well, there'll be a further 80 years all the way to 2105 without any testing. To all the states represented here today, let's work together to make that happen. Thank you.

I thank the Executive Secretary of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization. I give the floor to Ms. Vivian Okeke, Director of the International Atomic Energy Agency Liaison Office in New York, on behalf of Mr. Raphael Mariano Grossi, Director General of the Agency.

Mr. President, Secretary General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, on behalf of the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency, Mr. Rafael Mariano Grossi, I would like to commend the President of United Nations General Assembly, His Excellency, Mr. Phil Mon Young, for convening this high-level plenary meeting of the General Assembly in observance of the International Day against Nuclear Tests in 2025. I also thank USG and High Representative Izumi Nakamitsu and Professor Robert Floyd, Executive Director of CTBTO, for their statements. We commend the Government of Kazakhstan and other like-minded countries for their commitment over the years to the promotion of the observance of the International Day Against Nuclear Tests, some having experienced firsthand the devastating effects of nuclear testing on their territories. Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, since its establishment, the IAEA has worked to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons while making nuclear science and technology available for peaceful purposes, especially in low and middle income countries. Nuclear science and technology diagnose and cure diseases such as cancer, feeds the hungry, protects the environment, and provides clean energy that powers progress. In 2024, The IAEA Technical Cooperation Programme supported 151 countries and territories, 36 of them least developed, in tackling some of their most pressing challenges. As we mark the observance of the International Day Against Nuclear Tests, the IAEA continues to assist States to characterize residual radioactivity in areas affected by nuclear weapons tests. to assess whether the safe use of such land is possible or if remedial actions are needed. The IAEA continues to implement a project focused on strengthening national capabilities to assess the feasibility of releasing parts of the Semipalatinsk test site to normal economic use. The work will continue in the years to come And serves as a strong reminder of the long term hazards, thus a first of nuclear weapon testing. Mr. President, Excellencies, since his assumption of office in December 2019, Director General Grossi has taken an invigorated and strategic approach to the peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology to maximize impact by launching major initiatives, Rays of Hope, Zodiac, NUTEK Plastics, Atoms for Food, Maria Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Program, and the Liza Maitani Program. These initiatives are delivering tangible results for member states supported by growing international partnership and resource mobilization. Rays of Hope, for instance, is actively addressing the global gap in cancer care with more than 90 member states having requested assistance. Included in our wide-ranging work has been the provision of linear accelerators to Kenya, Malawi, and the Republic of Niger, and spec safety machines to the Republic of Benin and the Republic of Senegal. In July this year, Director General Grossi visited Ethiopia, Rwanda, Malawi, Kenya and Liberia to engage with local leaders and make tangible contributions to their cancer strategies, as well as discussing other ways the IAEA can support their development and also in areas such as energy and food security. Through the Zoonotic Disease Integrated Action, ZODIAC, launched amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the IAEA continues to support animal and human health for effective pandemic preparedness. By the end of last year, a total of 121 Member States had designated Zodiac National Coordinators and 129 member states had Zodiac National Laboratories. More than 50 Zodiac National Laboratories have received equipment and training and are now fully equipped for serology and molecular diagnosis or genetic sequencing. Meanwhile, the IAEA continues to support its member states in tackling plastic pollution through NUTEC Plastics. 104 member states now monitor microplastics, while 42 are developing radiation-based recycling. Our Atom for Food initiative, together with the Food and Agriculture Organization, is ramping up with 23 countries now participating. Atoms for Food has delivered laboratory equipment to sustain countries in Asia and the Pacific, and mobilized funds to address the re-emergence of the new world screwworm in Latin America. Mr. President, Excellencies, it is essential that nuclear technology is used safely and securely. While nuclear safety and security are national responsibilities, the IAEA serves as an international forum in which countries work together to develop safety standards and security guidelines. The IAEA helps Member States to fulfill their nuclear safety responsibility by developing safety standards that may be used as a basis for national regulation and by providing, upon request, A variety of services, including expert review missions. In 2024, IAEA conducted 56 peer review and advisory services. To better assist member states in preparing for security challenges posed by non-state actors, In October 2023, the IAEA inaugurated its Nuclear Security Training and Demonstration Center as part of IAEA Laboratories Complex in Seibersdorf. It is the world's first international training center dedicated to enhancing global security. Through practical hands-on training in critical areas such as the physical protection of nuclear facilities, nuclear forensics, and cybersecurity, the center helps to strengthen member states' abilities to tackle nuclear terrorism and address unique challenges and implement complex projects on nuclear security. So far, the new center has held more than 70 training events with over 1,000 participants. Another core function of the IAEA is to verify that countries are not working to acquire nuclear weapons. Agency inspectors conduct verification in nuclear facilities all over the world. The number of states with safeguards agreements in force is now 191, and 144 of the states have additional protocols in force, giving the agency greater access to location and information. When the DG took office in 2029, then NPT non-nuclear weapons states parties had not yet brought comprehensive self-gas agreements into force, and now there are only three remaining. In line with relevant decisions of the IAEA Board of Governors and the General Conference, the Director General has also encouraged States without APs to conclude and bring into force APs and called upon States with small quantities protocols to amend or resign them as they are no longer adequate for the current safeguard system. We also support States in their effort to create and implement nuclear weapons free zones, which already cover vast regions of the world. Mr. President, Excellencies, as I conclude, let me reaffirm the IAEA's firm commitment to contribute to a world free of nuclear weapons and nuclear tests by exercising credible nuclear verification and by promoting effective nuclear safety and security and assisting states in the remediation of land areas damaged from hazardous effects of nuclear testing The IAEA is making a tangible contribution towards this end. I thank you.
I thank the Director of the International Atomic Energy Agency Liaison Office in New York. I give the floor to Ms. Oemwa Johnson, Youth Representative from Kiribati.

President of the General Assembly, Under-Secretary-General for Disarmament Affairs, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, my name is Zoema Johnson, a youth from the Republic of Kitts and Nevis. I am honored to speak on behalf of the Nuclear Age Peace Foundation and its youth initiative, Reverse the Trend. at the high-level meeting to commemorate the International Day Against Nuclear Tests, an initiative spearheaded by Kazakhstan. I also stand here as a fourth-generation nuclear survivor from Christmas Island, a living embodiment of the long-lasting consequences of nuclear testing. My presence here underscores the urgent need for acknowledgement and action regarding the ongoing implications of these tests on our health, our environment, and our very existence. I speak today with urgency and hope on behalf of survivors and young people for a future free of nuclear weapons, a future that is both necessary and inevitable. Nuclear weapons use including nuclear weapon testing, left an indelible mark on affected communities, particularly on the people of Kiribati. The United Kingdom and the United States detonated nuclear bombs at Christmas Island, resulting in generations living with poisoned soil and cancers. President and distinguished delegates, When I speak of nuclear testing, I do not speak from history books. I carry the voices of my ancestors and the lived pain of my family. Between 1957 and 1962, as part of Operation Grebble, the United Kingdom and the United States conducted some of the most powerful thermonuclear detonations on Keesma. My great-grandfather, Pauro Tagatea, and my grandfather, Metua Pauro, who was only 14 when they lived through those bombings. They had no shelter, no real protection. Instead, they were given only a thin blanket to cover their eyes against the blinding flashes. The smallest tennis court on the island, which was used as a gathering space, was not large enough for everyone. Some villagers were sent away on boats to nearby islands to make room, while others remained exposed on Keshmas, forced to crouch under the sky as fireballs lit up the sky and shook the earth beneath their feet. Radiation exposure left my grandfather with lasting health issues, hearing loss, memory decline, and conditions never before seen in our family. Other nuclear survivors have also experienced the same conditions and even extreme health complications. The intergenerational effects are undeniable. Two of my father's older siblings were born prematurely and died shortly after birth. His older sister, the one born just before him, died at the age of 18 after suffering from an undiagnosed neurological illness and a known but severe headache. My father also suffers from chronic migraine, and I too have experienced chronic migraines and other unexplained health conditions. This is not the past, it is the present. It is my people's and my family's reality. And it is why I stand before you today to remind this assembly that nuclear weapons have poisoned our land, ocean, and bodies. They destroy lives across generations. My community should serve as a stark reminder that nuclear weapons can never be justified as abstract security tools. The Pacific Islands did not choose to become a laboratory of destruction, and the suffering imposed by colonial powers detonating their radioactive bombs is inseparable from histories of domination and disregard for human dignity. President and distinguished delegates, in this struggle for the total and irreversible elimination of nuclear weapons, The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons emerged as a landmark of nuclear disarmament and is one of the only disarmament treaties in which affected communities and civil society are meaningfully included. Articles 6 and 7 of the treaty also reframe nuclear disarmament as both a humanitarian and environmental imperative, adding urgency for all states to join the treaty without delay. Furthermore, we view environmental remediation as central to nuclear disarmament, as we cannot speak of disarmament without addressing the poisoned waters and irradiated lands, all of which left behind an intergenerational health crisis. Nuclear justice means cleanup. reparations and victim assistance in addition to the total and irreversible elimination of nuclear weapons. In this regard, I am grateful to both Kazakhstan and my state, Kyrgyzstan, for spearheading efforts on establishing an international trust fund for the victims of nuclear weapons. An international trust fund is urgently needed to help victims. It must be established as soon as possible. We, the victims, cannot wait for more negotiations. President and distinguished delegates, we must also reconcile the gendered impacts of nuclear weapons use and testing. Feminist approach insists that human security must guide our policy, not militarized power, as women are disproportionately affected by radiation exposure. Women in Kismes and other affected Pacific islands, such as the Marshall Islands and French Polynesia, as well as in impacted regions in Algeria, Kazakhstan and North America bore disproportionate burdens, miscarriages, birth defects, and long-term reproductive health complications. The abolition of nuclear weapons protects the principles of gender equality and dismantles systems of domination over care. The fallout struck most deeply to mothers and children. At the same time, women are historically excluded from decision-making, yet they emerged as some of the strongest advocates for truth, care, and nuclear disarmament. Their leadership demonstrates that a feminist approach to disarmament is essential, one that centers human security, equality and care, not militarized power. President and distinguished delegates, the abolition of nuclear weapons, in the words of former UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon, is no longer a dream. It is the unfinished business of decolonization. We are not prepared to inherit a legacy of complacency, nor can we continue to live in the shadow of these weapons. Thank you.
I thank Ms. Johnson. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Guinea, who will speak on behalf of the African States.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the African Group. The African Group expresses appreciation to the President of the General Assembly for convening this meeting and to the Secretary-General of the United Nations for his message and valuable support towards nuclear disarmament. The fact that this year marks eight years since the first nuclear weapons were tested and the first nuclear detonation occurred in Hiroshima and Nagasaki is a stark reminder of the existential threat posed by the use and testing of nuclear weapons, not only to humanity, but international peace and security. The group is concerned that nuclear tests have continued and that more than 2,000 tests have been conducted worldwide. As we convene here today, we shall reaffirm our determination to raising awareness and preventing the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of the use and testing of nuclear weapons. An end to nuclear tests is a necessary measure pending the total elimination of nuclear weapons. Mr. President, the total elimination of nuclear weapons remains the only absolute guarantee against their use or threat of use. In this context, the Group reiterates that the humanitarian consequences and risks associated with nuclear weapons underpin the moral and ethical imperatives for nuclear disarmament and the urgency of achieving and maintaining a nuclear weapon free world. The group wishes to emphasize humanitarian consideration in the context of all deliberation on nuclear weapons, particularly its serious concern over the catastrophic consequences of the use or detonation of nuclear weapons, either by accident or as a deliberate action. We call on all States, particularly nuclear-armed States, to take into consideration the humanitarian consequences of the use and testing of nuclear weapons on human health, the environment and vital economic resources, among others, and to take necessary measures aimed at dismantling and renouncing these weapons. The group supports the principle of complete nuclear disarmament as the utmost prerequisite for maintaining international peace and security. It is in this spirit that we recall the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, NPT, as well as the entry into force of the landmark Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapon, TPNW, which seeks to advance nuclear disarmament and to comprehensively prohibit nuclear weapons tests. In this regard, the group wishes to urge nuclear-armed states and those under the so-called nuclear umbrella to seize the opportunity to sign and ratify the TPNW at an early date, as well as pursue the goal of a nuclear-weapon-free world. The group expresses deep concern about the rapid advancement of technology, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence, and the associated risk of automatic decision-making processes related to nuclear testing, which could lead to irreversible decisions. Mr. President, the African group supports the goals of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, CTBT, which seeks a comprehensive ban on nuclear tests with all their attendant humanitarian and environmental ramifications, as well as to cease all vertical and horizontal proliferation of nuclear weapons. The Group takes note of the Conference on Facilitating Entry into Force of the CTBT during the high-level week of the 78th session of the General Assembly, and looks forward to the upcoming conference to be held later this month in New York. The group wishes to reiterate the importance of achieving universal adherence to the CTBT, taking into consideration the special responsibilities of armed states, and calls upon Annex II states to sign and ratify without further delay and without preconditions. The group believes that the CTBT offers hope of halting further development of -- or proliferation of nuclear weapons, thereby contributing to the goal of nuclear disarmament. In conclusion, Mr. President, the African Group once again calls on all states to work persistently to facilitate the expeditious entry into force of the CTBT to fulfill the goals and objectives of a nuclear weapons free world, taking into account the special responsibility of the nuclear armed states.

I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Guinea. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia, who will speak on behalf of the community of Latin American and Caribbean states.

Mr. President, I have the honor to address this high-level plenary meeting on behalf of the 33 member states of the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, CELAC. CELAC recalls resolution 64/35 of December 2009, and resolution 72/51 of December 2017, both adopted by the General Assembly, by which 29th of August was declared the International Day Against Nuclear Tests, with the aim of raising awareness and promoting education on the effects of nuclear weapons test explosions or any other nuclear explosions, and on the need for their cessation as one of the means to achieve the goal of a world free of nuclear weapons. CELEAC reiterates its firm support for the commemoration of the International Day against Nuclear Tests and upholds all international initiatives against nuclear testing. since we understand that nuclear explosions of all kinds, as well as other non-explosive nuclear tests aimed at developing and improving weapon capabilities, endanger human life, have disastrous long-term environmental consequences, and exacerbate geopolitical tensions. thereby threatening international peace and security. The states that make up CELAC agree that the mere existence of nuclear weapons represents a threat to humanity and that the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons constitutes a crime against humanity and a violation of international law, including international humanitarian law and the Charter of the United Nations. We therefore issue a strong appeal for States to refrain from conducting nuclear tests, as well as other nuclear explosions or any related experimental testing anywhere in the world. including subcritical tests and those carried out through simulations intended to develop and enhance nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction. This contravenes the spirit and purpose of the Treaty of Non-Proliferation as well as the purpose and the provisions contained in the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons and the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. CELAC expresses its appreciation to the 187 States that have signed and the 178 that have ratified the CTBT. And in this regard, we welcome the fact that Latin America and the Caribbean is the only region in the world in which all states have ratified this instrument, thereby reinforcing the region's support for nuclear disarmament and the international non-proliferation regime. Celec reiterates the importance and urgency of the treaty's entry into force and urges those states that have not yet signed or ratified it, particularly those whose ratification is indispensable for its entry into force, to do so without further delay. Our region promotes respect for the sovereignty of all states. and in advocating for non-proliferation policies, our region reaffirms that such policies must not undermine states' rights to develop nuclear science and technology for safe and peaceful purposes. In this regard, CELAC highlights the work of the International Atomic Energy Agency IAEA as well as that of its Director General, Latin American Rafael Grossi, in promoting the development of nuclear capacities for CELAC members in the areas of health, food security, and agriculture, radiological technology, education, radiation protection and safety, environmental applications, energy, and other areas of nuclear technology for peaceful purposes. We're committed to strengthening existing regional capacities, in particular through the regional cooperative agreement for the promotion of nuclear science and technology in Latin America and the Caribbean, ARCAL. with a view to providing concrete responses to the challenges of its application in the fields of health, agriculture, food security, the environment and energy, among others. Mr. President, no state must ever employ nuclear weapons under any circumstances, and we reiterate that the use or the threat of use of such armaments as we have already underscored, constitutes a crime against humanity and an abhorrent violation of international law. States must respect and fully comply with the obligations and provisions contained in the various instruments that make up the disarmament and non-proliferation regime, including the NPT, the TPNW, and the CTBT, which has been and continues to be a fundamental component in the efforts to achieve complete nuclear disarmament and has received overwhelming support from the international community. Furthermore, the states of CELAC are parties to the Treaty for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, in Latin America and the Caribbean, the Treaty of Tlatelolco of 1967, which established the first nuclear weapons free zone, NWFZ, in a densely populated region of the world. We wish to pause briefly at this point to acknowledge Ambassador Flavio Roberto Bonzanini, who will conclude his mandate as Secretary General of the Agency for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean, OPANAL, at the end of 2025. His work has been of great importance for the consolidation of the Agency and the implementation of the Treaty of Tlatelolco. It is important to recall that our region was proclaimed a zone of peace on the basis of respect for the principles and norms of international law through the declaration we adopted in Havana in 2014. CELAC likewise reiterates the continuing validity of the declarations on nuclear disarmament adopted by the community on the 20th of August of 2013 in Buenos Aires Argentina 29th of January 2014 in Havana Cuba 29th of January 2015 in Belen Costa Rica to the 27th of January 2016 in Quito Ecuador 25th of January 2017 in Punta Cana Dominican Republic on the 24th of January 2023 in Buenos Aires Argentina and on the 1st of March 2024 in Kingston, Jamaica. We take note of the third meeting of states parties of the TPNW held from the 3rd to the 7th of March 2025 in New York. We encourage those states that have not yet ratified the treaty to do so without delay, thereby contributing to international peace and security. Mr. President, We urge nuclear weapon states to fulfill their unequivocal commitment to eliminate their nuclear arsenals under Article VI of the NPT, as well as their obligations arising from that treaty. We also express our disappointment at the consecutive failure of the ninth and tenth NPT review conferences to adopt a consensual final document. I thank the distinguished representative of Iraq. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Germany, speaking on behalf of the Group of Friends on the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I am delivering this statement on behalf of the Friends of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, Australia, Canada, Finland, Germany, Japan, and the Netherlands. We thank the president of the General Assembly for convening this meeting. 80 years have passed since the world witnessed the first nuclear test, and then the decades that followed, more than 2,000 tests took place. At the height of the Cold War, few would have believed it possible that in the 21st century, nations would come together to prevent another wave of testing. Yet we have. And today, looking back across those eight decades, we can say with confidence that the CTBT stands as one of the clearest demonstrations of what international cooperation can achieve. The CTBT is a core element of the international nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime. The norm against nuclear testing is one of the most widely accepted and most effective contributions of the CTBT in countering nuclear proliferation, as well as in containing and reducing nuclear threats. Achieving a safer world without nuclear weapons begins with an effective universal and verifiable commitment to a world free of nuclear testing, a world where everyone can be reassured that moratoria on nuclear tests are being maintained. What makes the CTBT so successful is that it is not just a piece of paper. The CTBT is backed by the International Monitoring System, IMS, a truly global network reaching all the way to Antarctica that works every day quietly and efficiently to make sure no nuclear test explosion goes unnoticed. It is a transparent system where every participating country sees the same data. That openness builds trust and makes it far harder for anyone to conduct a secret nuclear test. In an age where misinformation spreads faster than facts, the IMS gives us hard evidence that everyone can rely on. It is worth noting that the monitoring system's technical assets also have diverse scientific and civil applications that benefit all states, including monitoring nuclear accidents and detecting volcanic activity, earthquakes, and tsunamis. The CTBT has been instrumental in creating and promoting the global norm against nuclear testing. Its verification regime has so far successfully detected every declared nuclear test. We recall our condemnation of the six nuclear tests conducted by the DPRK since 2006 and strongly urge the DPRK not to conduct further testing, fully comply with all the relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions, and to take concrete actions towards the complete, verifiable, and irreversible dismantlement of its nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, and related programs. We reiterate that any new DPRK nuclear test would be irresponsible, unacceptable, and in violation of UN Security Council resolutions. We reaffirm that the DPRK cannot and will never have the status of a nuclear weapon state in accordance with the NPT, nor any special status of any kind. We call on the DPRK to sign and ratify the CTBT as a matter of priority. Pending the entry into force of the treaty, we call upon all states to declare or maintain their existing national moratoria on nuclear weapon test explosions and any other nuclear explosions as an example of responsible international behavior that contributes to international peace and stability, and to refrain from any action that would undermine the treaty's objective and purpose. 80 years after the first nuclear test, it is worth remembering that we did not get here by chance. Maintaining the IMS has required steady commitment, resources, and consistent technical upkeep. If we allow it to degrade, we risk undoing decades of progress and may have to rebuild capabilities that took years to develop. Eight decades on, the choice is clear: keep the system strong, reliable, and ready to detect nuclear tests, thereby strengthening the norm against testing. It is crucial that efforts to preserve and sustain this key asset commence without delay. In this context, we stress the importance of individual States' financial commitments and contributions by States signatories to ensure the completion, maintenance and pending long-term sustainment of the IMS. We reaffirm our continued commitment for maintaining the long-term sustainability of all elements of the verification regime pending the entry into force of the treaty. We look forward to the integrated field exercise in Namibia in 2026 and thank our Namibian colleagues for their readiness to host the exercise. The IFE will further strengthen the CTBTO's on-site inspection capabilities as the ultimate verification measure once the treaty enters into force. We also applaud the persistent and impressive efforts of the Executive Secretary of the CTBTO Preparatory Commission, Dr. Robert Floyd, and his team towards the universalization of the Treaty. Lastly, we would like to thank the Article 14 coordinators, Sweden and the Philippines, for their dedicated efforts. We look forward to the upcoming Article 14 Conference as an opportunity to advance our shared goal of bringing the treaty into force. The CTBT's value is unquestionable, and its successes are already visible. But we cannot take it for granted. We cannot take for granted the global norm against nuclear testing until it is legally binding. As such, we urge all states that have not already done so to sign and ratify the treaty, and particularly the now nine Annex II States, and encourage State signatories to support continued efforts to strengthen the Treaty and its verification regime and to achieve its entry into force as soon as possible. Thank you very much.

The TPNW also prohibits nuclear tests, which therefore strengthens the global norm against nuclear testing in full complementarity with the CTBT. We welcome the important progress made towards universalization of the CTBT and recognize the importance of the ratifications by Somalia, Dominica, Equatorial Guinea, Gambia, Timor-Leste, Tuvalu, Sao Tome and Principe, Solomon Islands and Sri Lanka since the 2021 Conference on Facilitating the Entry into Force of the CTBT. I thank you.

Costa Rica.
