As co-chair, Australia convened the 11th meeting of the Friends of the CTTB last year, which brought together 50 states to reiterate their shared commitment to the treaty. 86 states and one observer associated with the joint ministerial statement of the CTTB friends, underlining the unquestionable value of the treaty and commending the continued efforts to bring it closer to universality. We look forward to supporting the adoption of the final declaration during the Article 14 Ministerial Conference on Facilitating Entry into Force of the CTBT under the co-presidency of the Philippines and Sweden. We thank them for their ongoing commitment and valuable work. The entry into force of the CTBT as a universal and verifiable ban on any nuclear explosions should be achieved without delay. Australia continues to urge all states that have not yet done so to sign and ratify the CTBT without further delay or precondition, particularly the nine Annex II states required for its entry into force. Finally, Australia congratulates Dr Robert Floyd on his reappointment as Executive Secretary of the CTBT O's Preparatory Commission, which is a tribute to his determined and persistent efforts on behalf of the treaty. His efforts have been instrumental in upholding the global norm against nuclear testing. Thank you, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kazakhstan.

Mr. President, Madam High Representative, Executive Secretary Floyd, Excellencies, today at the 15th commemoration of the International Day Against Nuclear Tests, we gather not only to recall the past, but to accept responsibility for the future. For Kazakhstan, this day is part of our national conscience. It recalls the suffering of Semipalatinsk, where more than 450 nuclear explosions scarred our land and people. Most of all, it affirms the resolve that from such tragedy, a different path must be chosen. On 29th August, 1991, Kazakhstan closed the Semipalatinsk test site forever. With that sovereign act, we transformed the page of devastation into a page of hope and optimism. Soon after independence, we renounced the world's fourth largest nuclear arsenal. The legacy continues to define who we are and our commitment to disarmament. President of Kazakhstan, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, has unequivocally stated that tragedy of Semipalatinsk must never be repeated, calling for lasting peace and the complete ban on nuclear testing for the sake of future generations.

Yet today, the global landscape is deteriorating.

More than 12,500 nuclear warheads remain, with nearly 2,000 of them on high alert. Arms control agreements are eroding. Arsenals are being modernized. Adding to those challenges is the intrusion of artificial intelligence into nuclear decision-making. Algorithms devoid of conscience must never be allowed to shape decisions of war and peace. Against this backdrop, last week in Astana, Kazakhstan, as one of the founding states of the Semipalatinsk Treaty, hosted a dialogue on negative security guarantees in the context of nuclear weapon-free zones, a reminder that remembrance must be matched by action. This day is about people. Survivors of Semipalatinsk and other test sites remind us constantly that human cost and pain endure across generations, as we heard it very clearly today from the survivor from Kiribati. Their testimony underscores that disarmament is not only a strategic requirement, but a moral imperative. Together with Kiribati, Kazakhstan continues to advocate for justice and support for affected communities. Together, we have proposed establishing the International Trust Fund for Victim Assistance and Environmental Remediation. Distinguished delegates, the International Day Against Nuclear Tests is not only a moment of remembrance, it is a call to sustain moral responsibility. Kazakhstan remains committed to the goal of a world free of nuclear weapons and to concrete steps that strengthen the global disarmament and non-proliferation regime. For Kazakhstan, it is clear that the CTBT remains the only legally binding instrument to end nuclear testing, and its entry into force is more urgent than ever. And we thank Dr. Floyd for his active work in this respect. Our shared duty is to turn the lessons of history into measurable progress, reducing nuclear risks upholding international law, and deepening cooperation among states. The legacy we must leave is one of responsibility, accountability, and foresight. We must prove that lasting security depends on dialogue, confidence, and the complete and permanent prohibition of nuclear weapons, their use, and testing. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kazakhstan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the People's Republic of China.

Mr. President, as the world grapples with a complex and profoundly evolving security landscape, as well as incessant regional flare-ups and geopolitical tensions, the nuclear disarmament process is under tremendous stress, raising the risks. of nuclear the risks, the international community must fully recognize the grave impact of nuclear weapons on the security of humankind and the environment and curb nuclear proliferation and prevent a nuclear war from the source with a view to laying a solid foundation for lasting peace and universal security. President Xi Jinping of China has put forward the Global Security Initiative advocating the principle of indivisible security and promoting a vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security. This initiative calls for the rejection of Cold War mentality and bloc confrontation and contributes fundamentally to improving security environment at the regional and international levels. President Xi pointed out that nuclear weapons are the sword of Damocles hanging above humanity and therefore should be comprehensively prohibited and ultimately eliminated for the realization of a world free of nuclear weapons. From the very first day China possessed nuclear weapons, it has undertaken never to be the first to use them at any time and under any circumstances. China unconditionally commits itself not to use or threaten to use nuclear weapons against non-nuclear weapon states or nuclear weapon free zones. China firmly upholds a nuclear strategy of self-defense. maintains its nuclear capabilities at the minimum level required for national security. China never participates in any form of arms race, does not provide nuclear umbrella to other countries, and does not deploy nuclear weapons on foreign soil. Regardless of how the international situation may evolve, China will remain steadfast in upholding these commitments.

Mr. President,

This year marks the 80th anniversary of the founding of the United Nations. For decades, the international arms control and non-proliferation regime has been continuously bolstered, playing a vital role in safeguarding global security and peace. The Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty as a key pillar of the international nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime. has made the complete prohibition of nuclear testing an irreversible trend of our times, therefore bringing humanity closer to the goal of banning and eliminating nuclear weapons entirely. Next year will mark the 30th anniversary of the CTBT's opening for signature. The prohibition of nuclear testing has become a widely shared consensus of the international community. All countries should resolutely safeguard the Treaty's crucial role in containing a nuclear arms race and reducing the risk of nuclear war, and working together to build a world of lasting peace and security for all. Nuclear weapon states should maintain their moratoria. reduce the role and significance of nuclear weapons in their respective national security strategies, and make unequivocal pledges not to be the first to use nuclear weapons. China was among the earliest signatories of the CTBT and remains the nuclear weapon state with the fewest nuclear tests. China has consistently upheld the purposes and objectives of the CTBT, honored its moratorium commitment, and supported relevant GA resolutions as well as Security Council Resolution 2310. China has established a national institution responsible for CTBT compliance preparations, actively participates in the work of the Preparatory Commission and has attended all conferences on facilitating the CTBT's entry into force. As the Treaty's second largest financial contributor, China has been working closely with the Provisional Technical Secretariat and completed the construction of 10 out of the 11 IMS stations hosted by China, demonstrating our firm support for the Treaty. China remains committed to working with all parties to promote the early entry into force of the CTBT and making unremitting efforts toward the noble goal of comprehensively prohibiting and ultimately eliminating nuclear weapons. Thank you, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of the People's Republic of China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Mr. President, honorable delegates, Mexico is grateful for the convening of this meeting and we'd like to align ourselves with the statements of Colombia on behalf of the community of Latin America and Colombian states and of Brazil, on behalf of the Agency for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean. We also thank Kazakhstan for its leadership in promoting this commemoration that reminds us of the urgent need to eliminate not only nuclear tests but in particular eliminate the totality of nuclear weapons which are the greatest existential threat facing humanity fortunately the territory of Latin America and the Caribbean have never been the scene of nuclear tests however the possibility of that happening was there for quite a long time. The countries of our region decided to demonstrate to the world that it was possible to take on the leadership in the area of disarmament by establishing the very first nuclear weapons free zone with the Treaty of Tlatelolco, of which Mexico is a proud depositary. The treaty has become a pillar of our permanent commitment to international peace and security. Now, the effects of nuclear tests on the planet are undeniable. The contamination of soil, of water-bearing strata, and of the atmosphere. These effects persist even today. The current global urgency to protect the planet in the face of environmental and climate crises that are unprecedented forces us or compels us to reiterate that a single nuclear test should never be allowed ever again. Now from a humanitarian perspective, nuclear tests had an impact on entire generations that were exposed to radiation and they were never warned of the terrible effects of that radiation. The scientific community has documented in a convincing fashion the differentiated impact of radiation on women and girls who confront greater medical and social risks to Recall these consequences of nuclear tests compels us as an international community to prevent their repetition. We'd like to underscore and reaffirm our conviction that nuclear tests should not be renewed for any reason and under any pretext. The Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty provides this guarantee through a legal framework and a global verification system. Mexico would like to make a firm appeal to all states that have not done so to sign and ratify the treaty without any further delays, preconditions or other conditionalities. The postponement of this ratification is unacceptable, as each year my country will present together with Australia and New Zealand the traditional resolution on that treaty, hoping to be able to count on the support of the entire membership of the UN for its adoption. We would also like to reaffirm the importance of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons that seeks to denounce and eliminate once and for all these lethal weapons. Both instruments are complementary and are essential in order to advance towards a world free of nuclear weapons. In the face of the impacts of rapid, exponential, I would say, technological change and the realities of the 21st century, my country will submit this fall a resolution in the first committee regarding the risks of incorporating artificial intelligence into the command and control systems of nuclear weapons. Mexico. would like to insist that the use of science and emerging technologies in the nuclear sphere must be exclusively geared towards peaceful goals such as healthcare, free and clean energy and sustainable agriculture. Furthermore, we consider it essential that initiatives are promoted on education and historical memory that make it possible to convey to new generations the consequences of nuclear tests and their impact on populations thus preserving the testimonies of victims so as to avoid that these tests are ever repeated. Lastly, Mexico would like to reiterate its commitment to continue working for a world free of nuclear tests and nuclear weapons, strengthening multilateralism and international law as pathways to ensure collective peace and security and the well-being of present and future generations. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Guatemala.

Guatemala would like to thank the President of the General Assembly for convening this high-level meeting to commemorate the International Day Against Nuclear Tests. We also recognize the valuable speeches by Dr. Floyd. as well as Ms. Okeke and Ms. Wewa Johnson. All efforts are critical to remind everyone about the urgent need to move towards the complete definitive prohibition of these practices, which have caused so much harm to humanity and to our world. Guatemala has condemned and will continue to condemn all nuclear tests because they represent a grave threat to international peace and security, and they also harm people's health, the health of the environment and sustainable development. Our experience has shown that it is the most vulnerable who have borne the brunt of the consequences of nuclear tests. It is deeply concerning that, In spite of the clear evidence that exists and documented evidence about the deleterious effects of nuclear tests on people and the environment, nuclear weapons states have still not shouldered their full responsibilities, nor have they shown any willingness to recognize the impact of their tests. And there is a lack of effective accountability mechanisms and specific measures geared towards reparation and redress. This raises major questions about their commitment to the principles of justice, equity, and international responsibility. Our country has a peaceful tradition, and we are committed to general complete disarmament, and that is why we have consistently supported multilateral efforts geared towards getting rid of nuclear tests. In line with this, we have ratified the CTBT and also the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. We are convinced that both instruments are fundamental steps towards achieving a world free of nuclear weapons. But we deeply regret the fact that More than 25 years on from the date when the CTBT was opened for signature, it still has not entered into force, and that is why we respectfully call on states who have not yet ratified it to do so without further delay, particularly those whose accession is critical. President, Nuclear tests are not matters of the past. As long as nuclear weapons continue to exist, the risk of new tests and a potential use, either accidental or deliberate, will continue to exist with potentially catastrophic consequences for humanity. That is why we reiterate our belief that the only way to guarantee international security is for nuclear weapons to be totally, verifiably and irreversibly eliminated. On this International Day, Guatemala joins the voices of the entire world who are clamoring for a future without nuclear weapons, guided by the principles of the United Nations Charter and by the inherent right of people to live in peace and security. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Guatemala. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Plurinational State of Bolivia.

President, distinguished representatives of member states, ladies and gentlemen, the Plurinational State of Bolivia, as a peace-loving state, wishes to reaffirm before this assembly in line with our political constitution which prohibits the manufacture and use of chemical, biological, nuclear weapons, that we are against all of these weapons and any kind of nuclear tests. We are a territory free of nuclear weapons and we reject the development and proliferation of nuclear weapons because they quite simply are contrary to life and humanity and Mother Earth. Bolivia is a peace-loving state and that is why we wish to join those commemorating this International Day today to remind the world that the scars of nuclear tests are long-lasting and their impacts can spread like a shadow of death that continues to affect future generations. Since 1945, more than 2,000 nuclear tests have been carried out in the world. They have contaminated land, water and the atmosphere, and they have seriously affected the health of entire communities, particularly women and indigenous people. Nuclear tests simply violate our harmony with nature and Mother Earth. These tests have wounded our planet, and they have made entire parts of the world uninhabitable, such as the Runit area in the Marshall Islands or the Hanford site. That is why we are committed to achieving denuclearization throughout the world. Thanks to the Tlatelolco Treaty, our region became the first zone, the first densely populated area to be fully free of nuclear weapons. This remains proof today that multinational diplomacy can prevail over destruction and the culture of death. Bolivia reaffirms its commitment to these efforts in which we participated as a key pioneer and proponent. As a result of this tradition, Bolivia would like to raise its voice to honor the life of and defend the sacred rights of our Mother Earth. We condemn nuclear tests and the consequences of them and we reaffirm our unwavering commitment to peace and harmony between humanity and nature. That is why we would like to come up with three concrete proposals. First, the universalization and immediate entry into force of the CTBT. This is a key priority. Secondly, we need to see the implementation of reparatory programs for regions that have previously been affected by nuclear tests and appropriate redress to all victims. Thirdly, we need to adopt a universal declaration that recognizes the rights of Mother Earth and prohibits any activity that causes ecocide as a new crime against life. President, today more than ever before we need to choose between the path of nuclear destruction or the path of life. Bolivia clearly chooses the latter. We need to protect our Pachamama, Mother Earth, for future generations so that they can live in peace and harmony with nature and without the scourge of war. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished Representative of the plurinational state of Bolivia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kyrgyzstan.

Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honor to deliver a statement on the event dedicated on to the International Day against nuclear tests. We would like to thank the brotherly Kazakhstan for initiative to declare this international day. This day serves as a powerful reminder of the humanitarian and environmental devastation caused by nuclear explosions. It also reaffirms our common duty to ensure that such tragedies never happen again. We were among the first states to sign and ratify the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. We firmly believe that CTBT's early entry into the force is vital for strengthening the global non-proliferation and disarmament regime. At the regional level, Kyrgyzstan is proud to be part of the treaty on nuclear weapon free zone in Central Asia, signed in Semipalatinsk in 2006. This historical agreement represents a significant contribution to global security and trust building. There is a need to educate the broad masses of society about the existing security architecture in the field of disarmament and non-proliferation, and efforts made by the UN member states, civil society, and the NGOs to shape and maintain peace on the planet. Our commitment to disarmament and non-proliferation has also found a strong multilateral recognition. Back in 2022, the UNGA unanimously supported the initiative of Kyrgyzstan to proclaim 5th of March as the International Day for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Awareness. We commemorate this day annually, raising awareness among the government, civil society, youth, and academia. Kyrgyzstan intends to support the contribution to increase the ability of future generations to live in a world free of nuclear weapons, annually observe the International Day, which promotes the significance of education in the field of disarmament and non-proliferation, encourage practical measures to implement the recommendations of the report of the UN Secretary General entitled United States Study on Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Education. Ladies and gentlemen, on this International Day Against Nuclear Tests, we gathered not only in remembrance, but in resolute commitment. My country will continue to work with all parties, states, and international organizations to achieve the goal of complete nuclear disarmament. We believe that only through joint efforts we build a world free from nuclear weapons. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kyrgyzstan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

Mr. President, thank you for your initiative in organizing this plenary meeting. Japan aligns itself with the statement delivered by Germany on behalf of the Friends of the CTBT. Let me also deliver a statement in our national capacity. This International Day against Nuclear Tests serves as a solemn reminder of the urgency to renounce nuclear tests across the globe and to take concrete and tangible measures toward a world without nuclear weapons. Our aspiration for that shared goal is stronger than ever, especially as we recently marked 80 years since the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki last month. Today, the global nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime faces unprecedented challenges. In the Pact for the Future, our leaders reaffirmed their strong commitment to eliminate nuclear weapons. and we must make every effort to bring that vision into reality. In this context, the early entry into force of the CTBT remains a priority for Japan. We urge all States, particularly the remaining States listed in Annex II, to sign and ratify the Treaty without further delay. Until that time, we urge all relevant states to declare or maintain existing moratoriums on nuclear weapon test explosions or any other nuclear explosions. Mr. President, we cannot overstate the vital role of the CTBTO's international monitoring system, including 10 monitoring sites in Japan, which serves as an effective deterrent against nuclear testing. Its global network has the capacity to detect suspected nuclear explosions worldwide. Japan has long supported this system by providing capacity building assistance to developing countries every year for the past 30 years. We also commend the steadfast leadership by Executive Secretary Dr. Robert Floyd, including his efforts to maintain and strengthen the IMS and promote the universalization of the CTBT. Mr. President, Japan expresses its serious concern over the advancement of North Korea's nuclear and missile development. and reaffirm its resolute commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions. We urge North Korea not to conduct any destabilizing or provocative actions, including a nuclear test. Japan also urged North Korea to comply with its obligation under the relevant UN Security Council resolutions, to return to full compliance with the NPT, and to sign and ratify the CTBT at earliest possible date. Mr. President, let us build on the momentum created by our meeting today. The upcoming conference on facilitating entry into force of the CTBT scheduled for September 26 presents another opportunity to further advance the universalization of the treaty. Japan will continue its contribution to constructive discussions, including at this conference, in pursuit of a world without nuclear weapons and testing. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cambodia.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of my ambassador who had a prior engagement. Mr. President, Excellency, distinguished delegates, Cambodia aligns itself with the statement delivered by Malaysia on behalf of ASEAN and wishes to add the following in our national capacity. At the outset, I would like to express my appreciation to you, Mr. President, for convening this important high-level meeting. I also wish to thank Ms. Izumi Nakamitsu, UN USG and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs and Dr. Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the CTBTO. This commemoration to promote the International Day Against Nuclear Tests is timely as our world facing increased nuclear risk. The resurgence of geopolitical rivalry and concerning reports of potential nuclear testing show that the dangers of the past are still with us. Mr. President, this year also marks the 80th anniversary of the first nuclear test. As Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has reminded us, we must never forget the legacy of more than 2,000 nuclear weapon tests carried out over the last eight decades. These tests left lasting damage to human health, the environment, and international trust. The consequences that continue to echo today. Against this backdrop, Cambodia underscores the urgent need to advance the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, CTBT, as both a legal obligation and a moral duty to protect humanity. We commend the tireless efforts of Dr. Robia Foye and the CTBTO Secretariat in promoting universalization and strengthening the verification regime, as well as the commitment of the many States that have ratified the Treaty. Yet, we remain gravely concerned that the CTBT has not entered into force because of the lack of ratification by a few key States. Cameroon strongly urges all Member States, especially those listed in Annex II, to seize the next year, 30th anniversary of the CTBT, as a historical opportunity to bring this landmark treaty into force. Mr. President, Cameroon reaffirms its steadfast support for the CTBT universalization and effective implementation. We also share ASEAN's commitment to preserving Southeast Asia as a nuclear-weapon-free zone under the Bangkok Treaty, reinforcing our regional and global efforts to advance disarmament and non-proliferation. In conclusion, Cambodia reaffirms its strong commitment to a world without nuclear weapons and testing. Let us unite with determination, solidarity, and shared responsibility to ensure nuclear testing become a thing of the past and never again threatening humanity's future. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cambodia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Republic of the Philippines.

Mr. President, the Philippines aligns itself with the statements of ASEAN and the group of friends of comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty as delivered by Malaysia and Germany. We join the international community in commemorating the international day against nuclear tests. We recognize the leadership of Kazakhstan in championing this initiative since 2010, building on the moral courage it demonstrated when it permanently closed the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site and voluntarily renounced nuclear weapons. We reaffirm the Philippines' unwavering commitment to nuclear disarmament. Nuclear weapons testing has left devastating humanitarian and environmental consequences. Entire communities continue to endure the intergenerational impact of radiation exposure, while fragile ecosystems remain scarred decades after testing has ceased. These enduring legacies remind us of our moral and legal responsibility to ensure that nuclear weapons are never used, tested, or developed again. In this regard, the Philippines recalls with support the adoption of the 2023 GA resolution titled Addressing the Legacy of Nuclear Weapons, co-sponsored by Kazakhstan and Kiribati. The resolution drew much needed international attention to the disproportionate humanitarian and environmental harm inflicted upon the world's most vulnerable populations. And it remains an important milestone in advancing a more just and human-centered discourse on nuclear disarmament. The Philippines continues to advocate for the universalization and early entry into force of the CTBT. Nearly three decades have passed since the treaty opened for signature, yet the treaty has yet to fulfill its promise due to the inaction of key states. We once again urge all remaining Annex II states to sign and ratify the CTBT without further delay. Until its entry into force, we call upon all states to maintain moratoria on nuclear test explosions. We also recognize the vital role of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization in developing and operating the world's most sophisticated nuclear test verification regime.

Through its global monitoring network.

The organization continues to build international confidence in compliance while demonstrating unequivocally that an effective, verifiable ban on nuclear testing is both technically feasible and operationally reliable. In this regard, we reaffirm our strong support for all the efforts of Dr. Robert Floyd and his team. Mr. President, Later this month, the Philippines is honored to co-preside together with Sweden the 14th Conference on Facilitating the Entry into Force of the CTBT, or the Article 14 Conference. As co-presidents, the Philippines and Sweden are determined to foster renewed international momentum for the treaty's entry into force and to encourage meaningful engagement from all states, especially the remaining Annex II states. Working closely with Sweden, the Philippines is committed to upholding the integrity of the CPT and to supporting consensus on a robust and forward-looking final declaration that reflects the urgent needs of the global community. We therefore call on all delegations to seize this opportunity in September to reaffirm collective support for the CPT. and to work together in advancing practical actions that can bring the treaty into force and strengthen the global norm against nuclear testing. Mr. President, the Philippines firmly believes that a world free of nuclear weapons is not merely an aspiration. It is an existential imperative for humanity's survival and our planet's preservation. The complete cessation of nuclear weapons testing represents an essential and achievable step towards that ultimate goal. We therefore renew our urgent call for the immediate end of all nuclear weapons test explosions and for substantive, measurable progress in nuclear disarmament.

The international community cannot afford further delay or half measures.

Only through decisive action can we secure a more stable, sustainable, and peaceful world for current and future generations.

Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Philippines. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Vietnam.

Mr. President, Vietnam aligns itself with the statement delivered by Malaysia on behalf of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Nearly three decades ago, the adoption of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty reflected the international community's resolve that nuclear explosions must never be carried out again, a resolve born from the deep scars of more than 2,000 nuclear tests and the collective hope for a world free of nuclear weapons.

Yet, that hope remains unfulfilled.

Today's commemoration is a sobering reminder of the challenges that persist. While the CTBT has reinforced the global moratorium on nuclear testing, it has not yet entered into force as a

legally binding instrument. Our world is no further removed from the threat of a nuclear war than it was three decades ago.

And efforts to remedy the long-term humanitarian and environmental consequences of nuclear weapon use and testing remain inadequate.

Against this backdrop, Vietnam reiterates its call for renewed efforts towards the complete and total elimination of nuclear weapons.

We urge all states who have not yet done so to sign and ratify the CTBT without delay. We also welcome the most recent signatory of Somalia and ratification by Papua New Guinea of the CTBT. Vietnam recognizes the CTBT organization and the International Atomic Energy Agency, IAEA,

for their work in raising global awareness of the dangers of nuclear testing,

monitoring and promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy worldwide. Vietnam reaffirms its commitment to nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation, and peaceful use of nuclear energy. We underscore the significance of the upcoming review conference of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 2026, whose success will require constructive engagement and recommitment to multilateralism and diplomacy.

Vietnam stands ready to work with all partners for the common goal of a world free of nuclear weapons.

We also echo the calls of ASEAN member states for support for the upcoming ASEAN-sponsored biennial resolution on the Treaty on the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon-Free Zone, and reaffirm our commitment to engage with all nuclear weapon states to resolve our outstanding issues in accordance with the objectives and principles of this treaty. Mr. President, Vietnam appreciates Kazakhstan's initiative to hold the International Day Against Nuclear Testing since it was first observed in 2010 and expresses solidarity to the victims and communities affected by the use and test of nuclear weapons. Their stories are reminders that our work is not about treaties alone, but also about protecting human lives and shared peace. The International Day Against Nuclear Testing is not just a commemoration,

It is a call to action to rekindle hope and fulfill our promise to a nuclear weapon free world.

I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Vietnam. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uruguay.

Thank you very much, President. Uruguay is grateful for the convening of this meeting and we acknowledge Kazakhstan's role in promoting the commemoration of this international day. This day reminds us of the importance of eliminating nuclear weapons and tests without further delay. We also fully align ourselves with the statement delivered by Colombia. speaking on behalf of CELAC. Uruguay is staunchly committed to the non-proliferation disarmament regime and we always have striven to achieve the goal of achieving a world free of nuclear weapons. That's why we've ratified all relevant instruments in this domain, particularly the CTBT. We adopted We signed the aforementioned convention in 1996 and we ratified it in 2001. We are concerned about the fact that it still has not entered into force as a result of some countries not ratifying it, and we urge those states to reverse their stance and to do so particularly in the current context. President, the only guarantee that there will be no more nuclear tests is to completely eliminate nuclear weapons. This has to be done in a transparent, irreversible, verifiable way within a clearly defined time frame. We welcome the efforts that have been made in the Pact for the Future which gives new momentum to commitments in the area of disarmament and promotes a world free of nuclear weapons. We hope this is reflected in the incorporation of more countries to the CTBT, and we hope that the co-chairs of the informal working group on universalization, together with Austria and New Zealand, will be able to move forward these efforts. Nevertheless, we think that states should have the right to peacefully use nuclear energy, particularly to boost areas such as health, food security and sustainable development within international security standards. We will continue to support all initiatives leading towards the complete elimination of nuclear weapons and to enhance the visibility of the regional organizations who have worked tirelessly towards achieving this goal. We have put forward the candidacy of Ambassador Juan Carlos Ojeda Villoni to be the Secretary General of OPANAL. Today more than ever we need to promote a climate of good faith and mutual respect based on the principles of the Charter and respect for international law. This requires serious commitments from the international community to achieve disarmament and global security. Lastly, on this International Day, we call on the entire international community to act responsibly. We cannot overlook the serious humanitarian consequences of nuclear tests, which particularly affect women, girls, vulnerable communities, and which jeopardize the well-being of future generations. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Uruguay. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ukraine.

Mr. President, on the occasion of the International Day Against Nuclear Tests, Ukraine joins the international community in commemorating all victims of nuclear explosions and reaffirms its commitment to a comprehensive legally binding prohibition of nuclear tests as a guarantee of strengthening international security. Ukraine believes that the CTBT is one of the key legal elements of the global security architecture in the field of nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation and serves as an essential instrument to establish a global standard against nuclear testing. As a responsible member of the international community, Ukraine ratified the CTBT in 2001 and has actively contributed to advancing its universalization and entry into force. We call upon all states that have not yet done so, in particular the remaining Annex II states, to sign and ratify the CTBT without any preconditions or further delay. Furthermore, we stress the importance for all states to maintain existing moratorium on nuclear testing, including by refraining from actions that could create conditions for their resumption. Ukraine supports the further strengthening of the CTPD verification regime, including the international monitoring system, the international data center, and onsite inspections as a guarantee of effective monitoring of compliance.

We would

like to draw the attention of UN member states to the fact that Ukraine certified primary seismic station PS45 Malin delivered seismic data to the international and national data centers at a rate of 99.99%. 59%. This level of availability sustained amid an ongoing war of aggression by the Russian Federation, including repeated missile and drone attacks, grid instability and physical damage risks, was enabled by the professionalisms of the PS45 operators and stations teams, as well as the step-by-step installation of guaranteed backup power at the station. Despite the war, Ukraine remains committed to ensuring reliable transmission of data from the Ukrainian seismic station. Mr. President, as the country that voluntarily gave up the third world's largest arsenal of nuclear weapons, and knowing that nuclear devastation is not only the legacy of past wars, Ukraine condemns any steps that undermine the established nuclear test ban regime, including the withdrawal of ratification of the CDBT and practices incompatible with the object and purpose of the treaty. In this regard, we strongly denounce the nuclear tests conducted by the DPRK. Ukraine urges North Korea to fully comply with its obligations under multiple UN Security Council resolutions to refrain from testing nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles. We also call upon Pyongyang to immediately return to compliance with the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and the IAEA Comprehensive Safeguards Agreements, as well as sign and ratify the Additional Protocol thereto, as well as the CTBT.
